html:
A genetically modified cotton that makes its own insecticide against the bollworm. India approved it for farming in 2002, and within about a decade it covered over nine tenths of the country's cotton fields.

The plant carries a gene from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, "Bt", that produces a protein toxic to certain caterpillars. Bollworms had become a plague in India, and farmers were spraying heavy doses of pesticide. The seed was sold by a joint venture of the Indian firm Mahyco and the American company Monsanto. Before approval, illegal Bt seed was already spreading in Gujarat.

Yields rose fast, and India became one of the world's largest cotton producers and exporters, in the land of the oldest cotton. But the story is disputed. Seed costs were high, the pink bollworm evolved resistance within some years, and pesticide use crept back up. Activists linked Bt cotton to debt and farmer suicides; most studies found no direct link but much hardship in rain-fed areas. It remains India's only approved genetically modified field crop, a lesson for debates after the Green Revolution.
sum: A genetically modified cotton that makes its own insecticide against the bollworm. India approved it for farming in 2002, and within about a decade it covered over nine tenths of the country's cotton fields.
